title: Release Barabbas (Luke 23:13–25)
hookLine: Pilate says three times he finds no fault, and yields to the shouts

lines: BACK FROM HEROD, IN THE ROBE.
cards: Pilate has already said it once: I find no fault in this man. He sent Jesus to Herod, and Herod sent him back, still in the gorgeous robe. So it's Pilate's problem again.

He calls together the chief priests, the rulers and the people, and gives the Roman governor's verdict. A verdict is supposed to settle things: someone in charge knows the right answer and says it out loud.
What happens next is a story about what that answer is worth when the room gets loud, and keeps getting louder.

teach.h: I FIND NO FAULT IN HIM.
teach.b: Pilate says it plainly: I've examined him, and I find no fault in him. Neither did Herod. I'll have him beaten, and let him go.
And the crowd cries out, all together: away with this man, release unto us Barabbas. Luke tells us who Barabbas is: a man thrown in prison for an uprising in the city, and for murder.
Pilate speaks to them again, wanting to release Jesus. They shout, crucify him.

Then, in the King James words: "And he said unto them the third time, Why, what evil hath he done? I have found no cause of death in him: I will therefore chastise him, and let him go." Three times, no fault.
Luke counts them so you'll notice.
"And they were instant with loud voices, requiring that he might be crucified. And the voices of them and of the chief priests prevailed." Not the evidence, not the law: the volume.

Pilate releases the man jailed for murder, and hands Jesus over to their will. Two things to hold carefully. First, this is one crowd before Pilate on one morning, with its leaders, not a whole people.

teach.h: I HAVE FOUND NO CAUSE OF DEATH IN HIM.
teach.b: Christians in the past used scenes like this to blame the Jewish people for Jesus's death, with terrible results, and churches, the Catholic Church among them, have since formally rejected that reading.
The sentence was Rome's, and the cross was a Roman punishment. Second, the man with the power knew the truth, said it three times, and gave it up.

how: In some churches the Passion is read aloud on Palm Sunday and Good Friday with the congregation speaking the crowd's lines, so that the shout belongs to everyone in the room rather than to someone else.

games.q: what's inside Luke 23:13–25 — tap the pairs.
p: in prison for uprising and murder
found no fault in him either

s: Pilate says he finds no fault in Jesus three times in Luke
Luke counts them: "he said unto them the third time, why, what evil hath he done?"
in Luke, Pilate is persuaded by new evidence
Luke says the voices prevailed. the verdict never changed; Pilate gave way.
the scene blames a whole people for Jesus's death
it describes a crowd and its leaders on one morning; the sentence and the cross were Rome's.

games.q: you're the governor. you've said three times the man is innocent. the crowd is shouting louder. what do you do?
o: release him, as your verdict says.
give the crowd what it wants.
send him back to Herod again.
games.why: "the voices of them and of the chief priests prevailed." Pilate releases Barabbas and delivers Jesus to their will.

practice: Think of something you know is right or true that you've gone quiet about because people around you are loud: at work, in your family, online, in your own head.
Say it to yourself plainly, three times, and notice whether it still feels true; you don't have to fight anyone, just don't hand it over. If you pray, you can ask God for steadiness.

wordCard.voice: Release Barabbas. The crowd's cry before Pilate: free the man jailed for uprising and murder, and crucify the one the governor found innocent.

orig.note: Greek: Barabbas. the name is often read as Aramaic bar Abba, son of the father, though Luke doesn't explain it.

carryVoice: Your line: three times, no fault. The truth was known, and the volume won. That's day five hundred eighty-four.
